title: The Digestive System
hook: From the first bite to the final absorption, your digestive tract is a one-way assembly line that turns food into fuel your cells can use.
key_points: The digestive system breaks food into nutrients the body can absorb.
Digestion is both mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymes, acid).
Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine.
The large intestine reclaims water and houses helpful gut bacteria.
content_html: Food can't help you until it's taken apart. The digestive system is the body's processing line, a long tube running from mouth to end that breaks every meal into molecules small enough to cross into the blood. Digestion starts the moment you take a bite — teeth grind the food while saliva begins chemically breaking it down.
extra_html: The work is both mechanical and chemical. Chewing and the stomach's churning physically smash food apart, while acid and enzymes split it into simple nutrients like sugars, amino acids, and fats. The real payoff comes in the small intestine, whose enormous folded surface absorbs most of those nutrients into the bloodstream for delivery throughout the body. What remains moves into the large intestine, which reclaims water and hosts trillions of helpful gut bacteria before waste is expelled. As the NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases explains, organs like the liver and pancreas pitch in with juices and enzymes to keep the whole line running.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

related.title: Enzymes: Life's Catalysts
related.hook: The chemical reactions that keep you alive would crawl too slowly to matter — enzymes speed them up millions of times without being used up themselves.

related.title: The Human Microbiome
related.hook: You're never alone: trillions of bacteria, fungi, and other microbes live in and on your body, and most of them are working in your favor.

related.title: The Circulatory System
related.hook: Your heart pumps blood through roughly 60,000 miles of vessels, delivering oxygen and fuel to every cell and hauling waste away — about once a minute.

flashcards.prompt: What is the digestive system's main job?
flashcards.back_html: To break food down into small nutrients the body can absorb and use for energy, growth, and repair — and to remove what's left over as waste.

flashcards.prompt: Where does most nutrient absorption take place?
flashcards.explanation_html: The small intestine's long, folded, finger-lined lining gives a huge surface area where most digested nutrients pass into the bloodstream.

flashcards.prompt: What does the large intestine mainly do?

choices.text: Absorbs water and hosts helpful gut bacteria
Breaks down most proteins and fats
Pumps blood to the rest of the body

flashcards.explanation_html: By the time food reaches the large intestine, most nutrients are gone; it reclaims water from the remaining material and is home to trillions of gut microbes.
